sec.title: Background
sec.p: Platinum-based chemoimmunotherapy is used as a first-line treatment for advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction (G/GEJ) adenocarcinoma under specific regulatory circumstances, but effectiveness is often limited by cumulative toxicity, particularly in older patients and those with stroma-rich metastases.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This single-arm, phase II trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of a platinum-free triplet regimen as first-line therapy in patients with metastatic or unresectable G/GEJ adenocarcinoma. Participants received intravenous tislelizumab (200 mg, day 1), nab-paclitaxel (100 mg/m², days 1 and 8), and oral S-1 (80–120 mg twice daily, days 1–14) every 21 days. Primary endpoints were objective response rate (ORR) and progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), surgical conversion rate, disease control rate (DCR), and safety.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Among 43 enrolled patients, the confirmed ORR was 81.4% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 66.60-91.61%) and the DCR was 90.7% (95% CI: 77.86–97.41%). The overall median PFS was 8.6 months (95% CI: 6.10-11.04), and the overall median OS for the ITT population was 20.1 months (95% CI: 17.69–22.45). In subgroup analyses, patients who underwent conversion surgery had significantly longer OS compared with those who did not (median 29.5 months vs. 18.3 months; hazard ratio [HR]: 0.42, 95% CI: 0.20–0.90; P = 0.050). Patients aged ≥ 65 years showed longer PFS (13.7 vs. 7.2 months; HR: 0.39, 95% CI 0.19–0.80; P = 0.006) and OS (29.2 vs. 16.4 months; HR: 0.42, 95% CI 0.20–0.88; P = 0.021) than those aged < 65 years. Eight patients (18.6%) underwent conversion surgery, with 2 achieving pathological complete response. Grade ≥ 3 treatment-related adverse events included neutropenia (9.3%), leukopenia (7.0%), and anemia (2.3%).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This triplet regimen of nab-paclitaxel, S-1, and tislelizumab showed encouraging antitumor activity with a manageable safety profile. These findings warrant further validation in phase III randomized controlled trials, and support this regimen as a potential strategy, especially for older patients who may be less tolerant of platinum-based therapies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Gastric and gastroesophageal junction (G/GEJ) adenocarcinoma remains a significant global health burden, with more than one million new cases diagnosed annually and poor survival outcomes in advanced stages [1–3]. Across many regions, the integration of platinum-based chemotherapy with anti-programmed death-1 (PD-1) inhibitors is used as a first-line option under specific regulatory circumstances (e.g., HER2-negative disease meeting PD-L1 combined positive score thresholds), but the long-term efficacy of such regimens remains limited due to cumulative toxicities (including nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity) that frequently lead to treatment discontinuation [4–6]. Furthermore, these regimens demonstrate limited activity in stroma-rich metastatic environments, such as the peritoneum and retroperitoneum, where impaired drug penetration contributes to therapeutic resistance [7, 8].

Taxane-based chemotherapy has shown the potential to enhance tumor immunogenicity and improve drug delivery in desmoplastic tumors. In particular, albumin-bound paclitaxel (nab-paclitaxel) facilitates gp60-mediated endothelial transcytosis and exhibits improved intratumoral accumulation compared to solvent-based formulations [9, 10]. Preclinical studies suggest that nab-paclitaxel can remodel the tumor microenvironment by depleting cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), thereby promoting T-cell infiltration and immune priming [11–13]. The oral fluoropyrimidine S-1, widely used in East Asia, induces immunogenic cell death through mitochondrial DNA stress and activation of the STING pathway, supporting its role in immunomodulatory chemotherapy backbones [14–16]. Tislelizumab is a next-generation PD-1 inhibitor engineered to minimize Fcγ receptor binding on macrophages, thereby reducing antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP) of activated T cells and potentially enhancing T-cell persistence in stroma-rich tumors. Recent phase III data (e.g., RATIONALE-305 trial) showed that tislelizumab plus chemotherapy improved survival versus chemotherapy alone in HER2-negative G/GEJ adenocarcinoma, particularly in PD-L1–positive subsets, supporting a PD-1-based backbone for combination strategies [17, 18].

Although both nab-paclitaxel and S-1 have demonstrated clinical activity in gastric cancer, their combination with a next-generation PD-1 inhibitor in a platinum-omitting setting has not been systematically studied. To address this gap, we conducted a prospective, single-arm, phase II clinical trial to evaluate the efficacy and safety of a triplet regimen consisting of nab-paclitaxel, S-1, and tislelizumab in previously untreated patients with advanced G/GEJ adenocarcinoma. This study aims to explore a rational, toxicity-sparing, and potentially practice-changing approach to first-line therapy in this population.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This study was an investigator-initiated, single-arm, single-center, phase II clinical trial conducted at The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University. We planned to enrol approximately 43 patients to estimate objective response rate (ORR) with adequate precision and to provide supportive time-to-event endpoints. Assuming a true ORR of 70% and a null ORR of 50%, a one-sample exact binomial test (two-sided α = 0.05) yields ~ 80% power with n ≈ 40; we targeted n ≈ 43 to accommodate non-evaluable patients (5–10%). Time-to-event endpoints were not powered for formal subgroup hypothesis testing. This study was approved by the ethics committee of The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University (No. ChiECRCT20220042). The study was conducted in accordance with the International Conference on Harmonization of Good Clinical Practice guidelines, the Declaration of Helsinki, and applicable local laws and regulations. All subjects provided written informed consent prior to enrollment. This study is registered with chictr.org.cn, ChiCTR2200062653.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Eligible patients were previously untreated and aged between 18 and 85 years with histologically confirmed G/GEJ adenocarcinoma. Patients had clinical stage cT4 and/or cN + M1 by enhanced computed tomography (CT)/Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) according to the eighth edition of the American Joint Committee on Cancer TNM staging system [19]. Tumors were determined unresectable before therapy as evaluated by surgeons. Further inclusion criteria were Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) of 0 or 1, adequate hematopoietic, hepatic, and renal functions.

Patients who experienced any active, known or suspected autoimmune diseases or had other primary malignancies at screening were ineligible for this study. Patients with active hepatitis B or C, chronic enteritis, prior allergy or intolerance to study drugs or their excipients, or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-positive were excluded from the study. Pregnant or lactating patients, as well as patients with childbearing potential who did not use contraception if sexually active, were also excluded. Key eligibility required at least one measurable lesion per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid tumors version 1.1 (RECIST v1.1) [20]. Patients with non-measurable disease only were excluded from efficacy analyses requiring target-lesion measurements; full criteria are in Doc. S1.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: Eligible patients received fixed-dose tislelizumab (200 mg) intravenously on day 1 of each cycle. Nab-paclitaxel (100 mg/m2) was administered intravenously on days 1 and 8 of each cycle. S-1 (80–120 mg) was administered orally twice daily on days 1–14 of each cycle. Each cycle spanned 21 days. Operations included total or distal gastrectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy; metastasectomy was considered in cases judged technically resectable with anticipated R0 status. Decision-making followed multidisciplinary team (MDT) review after 6–8 treatment cycles, requiring radiologic downstaging to resectability, absence of new lesions, ECOG PS 0–1, and adequate organ function. Patients deemed inoperable continued therapy until radiographic disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

Tumor responses were assessed by two independent Radiologists using RECIST v1.1 with MRI or CT at baseline and every 2–4 cycles. Response was defined as achieving complete response (CR) or partial response (PR), while non-response included stable disease (SD) and progressive disease (PD). Safety was assessed by treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) since the initiation of therapy until the last dose of therapy were graded according to the National Cancer Institute’s Common Toxicity Criteria for Adverse Events (NCI-CTCAE), version 5.0 [21].

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The criteria of dose modification or interruption were applicable and specified in the protocol. The first chemotherapy dose was allowed to fluctuate up to 10% of the recommended dosage depending on the patient’s general health status. A maximum of two dose reductions of chemotherapy (to 80% or even 60% of the initial dose and then discontinuation) was permitted when serious TRAEs occurred. The decision to discontinue medication was based on patients’ choices and investigators’ judgments.
The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR, calculated as the proportion of patients achieving CR and PR) and progression-free survival (PFS).

Secondary endpoints were surgical conversion rate, overall survival (OS, defined as the period from enrolment to all caused death), disease control rate (DCR, referred to the proportion of patients with CR, PR, and SD) and safety.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies [percentage (%)], and continuous variables were presented as medians with interquartile range (IQR) or range. Objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) were summarized with exact (Clopper-Pearson) 95% confidence intervals. PFS was defined as time from enrolment to radiographic progression per RECIST v1.1 or death from any cause, whichever occurred first; deaths without prior radiographic progression between assessments were counted as PFS events at the date of death. OS was defined as time from enrolment to death from any cause. PFS and OS were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Between-group comparisons were performed using log-rank tests, with Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon tests as sensitivity analyses emphasizing early events. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models (univariable unless otherwise specified). Exploratory multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were additionally fitted for the strongest univariable signals, with a limited number of covariates selected a priori to minimize overfitting. Covariates were chosen based on clinical plausibility and event counts and included age group, Lauren histologic subtype, and conversion surgery; additional variables (e.g., metastatic site or baseline neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio) were evaluated only when feasible. Adjusted HRs with 95% CIs are reported as exploratory estimates.

To mitigate immortal-time bias in surgery- and response-defined subgroup analyses, we performed exploratory landmark and time-dependent sensitivity analyses. For conversion surgery, a 6-month landmark was selected a priori to align with the planned multidisciplinary reassessment after 6–8 treatment cycles; for the OS landmark analysis, only patients alive at 6 months were included, and for the PFS landmark analysis, only patients alive and progression-free at 6 months were included. Survival was measured from the landmark onward, and patients were classified according to whether curative-intent conversion surgery had occurred by the landmark. In addition, conversion surgery was modeled as a time-varying covariate in Cox proportional hazards models using each patient’s observed surgery time. For response-defined subgroup analyses, a 3-month landmark was selected to align with the first scheduled radiographic assessment window. For the OS landmark analysis, only patients alive at 3 months were included, and for the PFS landmark analysis, only patients alive and progression-free at 3 months were included. Patients were classified according to whether a confirmed objective response had been documented by the landmark, using each patient’s observed time to first confirmed response. These analyses were exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

Standard errors and 95% CIs for survival probabilities were computed using Greenwood’s formula. Median survival times and their 95% CIs were obtained using the Brookmeyer-Crowley method. Landmark survival rates at 6, 12, and 18 months were reported with 95% CIs. Subgroup analyses were exploratory and hypothesis‑generating, with no multiplicity adjustment for multiple comparisons. The Full Analysis Set (PP/intent‑to‑treat, ITT) included all patients who received at least one dose; patients with non‑evaluable (NE) responses were counted as non‑responders for ORR and included in time‑to‑event analyses. The Per‑Protocol Set required at least one post‑baseline tumor assessment. The Safety Set included all treated patients. Two‑sided P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) was calculated as the absolute neutrophil count divided by the absolute lymphocyte count obtained from baseline blood tests before treatment initiation. Patients were stratified into high and low NLR groups using the median NLR value (3.22) of the study cohort as the cut-off.

All statistical tests were two-sided, with significance set at P less than 0.05. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS version 30. All analyses were conducted using R Statistics software version 4.5.0. and GraphPad Prism 10.1.2.

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: From April 2021 to October 2022, 52 patients were screened and 9 were excluded due to prior or concomitant systemic therapies not permitted by the protocol. A total of 43 patients with metastatic G/GEJ adenocarcinoma were enrolled and received study treatment. Of these, 27 patients discontinued combination treatment due to disease progression (n = 24) and withdrawal due to patient decision (n = 3). One patient underwent emergency palliative gastrectomy for gastric perforation and was not classified as conversion surgery. Eight patients (18.6%) Converted to surgical treatment and 7 patients (16.3%) continued to receive S-1 plus tislelizumab as maintenance treatment. Antitumor activity and safety were analyzed in 43 patients (Fig. 1).

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: In the ITT population, 35 (81.4%) had PR, four (9.3%) had SD, 3 (7.0%) progressed and 1 (2.3%) was unable to undergo efficacy assessment due to the COVID-19 pandemic and were counted as non‑responders for ORR. The overall confirmed ORR per RECIST v1.1 was 81.4% (95% CI: 66.60-91.61%), the DCR was 90.7% (95% CI, 77.86–97.41%). The median time to response (TTR) was 1.5 months (IQR, 1.4–1.8). The median duration of response (DoR) was 6.6 months (95%CI, 5.91–8.08) (Table 2). It is noteworthy that this calculation censors patients at the time of conversion surgery (n = 8), which may underestimate the true durability of response to the chemotherapy-immunotherapy regimen. sec.p: Subgroup ORRs were calculated among the 26 patients with both available PD-L1 CPS data and evaluable response; a total of 17 patients were excluded (16 due to missing CPS data and 1 due to non-evaluable response). In patients with CPS ≥ 10, the ORR was 100%, compared to 87.5% in those with CPS < 10. In patients with CPS ≥ 5, the ORR was 92.9%, compared to 91.7% in those with CPS < 5, they all showed no significant differences (P = 0.369 and P = 0.720, respectively). Patients older than 65 years, with stomach tumor location, mixed type, moderately differentiated degree or with retroperitoneal lymph nodes metastatic site showed a trend toward higher ORRs (Table S1).

Of the 43 patients, 1 (2.3%) patient underwent an emergency palliative distal gastrectomy due to gastric perforation after completing three cycles of treatment. Eight (18.6%) patients underwent radical gastrectomy; of these, 4 (50%) underwent total gastrectomy and 4 (50%) distal gastrectomy, and 2 also underwent synchronous liver metastasectomy because the hepatic lesions were judged technically resectable with anticipated R0 status. Pathological complete response (pCR) was confirmed in 2 (4.7%) patients, both of whom were disease-free at the last follow-up.

By the cut-off date of April 30, 2025, the median follow-up time was 19.0 months (range: 8.4–30.3). Among 42 evaluable patients, 31 progression-free survival (PFS) events (73.8%) and 31 overall survival (OS) events (73.8%) were observed. Median PFS was 8.6 months (95% CI, 6.10-11.04) (Fig. 4A), and median OS was 20.1 months (95% CI, 17.69–22.45) (Fig. 4B). Kaplan-Meier landmark survival probabilities for PFS at 6, 12, and 18 months were 67.9% (95% CI, 50.27%-80.39%), 28.6% (95% CI, 14.22%-44.86%), and 14.3% (95% CI, 4.64%-29.21%), respectively. The corresponding OS probabilities were 90.2% (95% CI, 76.06%-96.22%), 75.3% (95% CI, 58.87%-85.86%), and 57.7% (95% CI, 41.04%-71.21%). It should be noted that patients who achieved response and underwent conversion surgery (n = 8) were censored at the time of surgery in the analysis PFS.

sec.p: Subgroup analysis of PFS and OS were shown in the Figures S1 and S2. In exploratory subgroup analyses, patients aged ≥ 65 years had longer PFS (median 13.7 vs. 7.2 months; HR, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.19–0.80; P = 0.006) and OS (median 29.2 vs. 16.4 months; HR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.20–0.88; P = 0.021) than those aged < 65 years; responders had longer PFS than non-responders (median 8.8 vs. 3.1 months; HR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.16–1.56; P = 0.118), with early separation in a sensitivity analysis using the Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test (P = 0.011), but no significant difference in OS (median 20.1 vs. 14.7 months; HR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.29–2.66; P = 0.820); patients who underwent conversion surgery had longer OS (median 29.5 vs. 18.3 months; HR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.20–0.90; P = 0.050) and a corresponding PFS benefit (HR, 0.13; 95% CI, 0.06–0.28; P = 0.001); and patients with PD-L1 CPS ≥ 10 had numerically shorter PFS (median 6.7 vs. 7.2 months; HR, 2.70; 95% CI, 0.92–8.05; P = 0.071) and no significant difference in OS (median 24.0 vs. 18.3 months; HR, 2.00; 95% CI, 0.73–5.27; P = 0.180) compared with those with PD-L1 CPS < 10 (Fig. 5A-H). Subgroup analysis according to lauren’s classification (intestinal type vs. diffuse type) showed significant differences in terms of PFS (median 28.5 vs. 7.9 months, P = 0.023) and OS (median 24.0 vs. 14.0 months, P = 0.020) (Figure S3). There were no significant differences in terms of PFS and OS in patients with metastatic site (Figure S4), sex, differentiation degree and primary tumor location (Figure S5A-F). Meanwhile, there were no significant differences in terms of PFS (median 13.1 vs. 6.7 months, P = 0.064) and OS (median 19.0 vs. 19.5 months, P = 0.262) in patients with PD-L1 CPS < 5 than PD-L1 CPS ≥ 5 (Figure S5G, H).

sec.p: To further assess the strongest univariable signals, we performed exploratory multivariable Cox analyses with limited a priori covariate adjustment. After adjustment for selected clinicopathologic factors, the association between older age and improved survival remained directionally consistent (PFS adjusted HR 0.14; 95% CI, 0.04–0.56; P = 0.005; OS adjusted HR 0.46; 95% CI, 0.18–1.16; P = 0.101), and the association between conversion surgery and improved outcomes also remained directionally favorable (PFS adjusted HR 0.18; 95% CI, 0.04–0.84; P = 0.029; OS adjusted HR 0.46; 95% CI, 0.14–1.45; P = 0.184). These analyses were exploratory and should be interpreted cautiously. Full adjusted estimates are provided in Table S2.

To address potential immortal-time bias, we performed exploratory landmark and time-dependent sensitivity analyses for surgery- and response-defined subgroups (Table S3 and Figure S6, S7). In the 6-month landmark analysis, the association between conversion surgery and improved outcomes remained directionally consistent with the primary analysis, but the magnitude of effect was attenuated. Among patients eligible for landmark analysis, conversion surgery was associated with a numerically longer PFS from the landmark onward (HR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.11–2.10; P = 0.335), whereas the association with OS was also directionally favorable but not statistically significant (HR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.12–2.16; P = 0.360).

In a complementary Cox model treating conversion surgery as a time-varying covariate using the observed surgery times, conversion surgery remained associated with improved PFS (HR, 0.32; 95% CI, 0.11–0.95; P = 0.041), whereas the association with OS was directionally favorable but did not reach statistical significance (HR, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.14–1.15; P = 0.088).

By contrast, the apparent benefit observed in the responder versus non-responder comparison was not retained in the 3-month landmark analysis based on each patient’s observed time to first confirmed response. Among patients eligible for landmark analysis, response status was not associated with significantly prolonged PFS (HR, 1.61; 95% CI, 0.49–5.35; P = 0.434) or OS (HR, 1.75; 95% CI, 0.53–5.81; P = 0.361). These findings suggest that the unadjusted responder/non-responder comparisons were influenced, at least in part, by time-dependent bias and should be interpreted cautiously.

We retrospectively included 42 patients with available baseline blood index data, including neutrophils and lymphocytes, who received the treatments. The NLR cut-off for stratification was set at the median value of the cohort (3.22), with NLR > 3.22 defined as high and NLR ≤ 3.22 defined as low. Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated the impact of NLR on PFS and OS (Figure S8A, B). Patients with high NLR had a shorter median OS than those with low NLR (16.4 months vs. 22.2 months, P = 0.061). However, no significant difference in PFS was observed between the high and low NLR groups (7.2 months vs. 13.1 months, P = 0.198).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were comprehensively evaluated in 43 patients (Table 3). Hematological toxicities predominated, with anemia (all grades: 74.4%; grade 1: 72.1%, grade 4: 2.3%) being the most frequent event. Leukopenia (decreased WBC count) occurred in 34.9% of patients (grade 1: 27.9%, grade 3: 4.7%, grade 4: 2.3%), followed by neutropenia (all grades: 18.6%; grade 3: 7.0%, grade 4: 2.3%) and thrombocytopenia (all grades: 14.0%; grade 2: 7.0%, grade 4: 2.3%). No cases of febrile neutropenia were observed.

sec.p: Gastrointestinal TRAEs included vomiting (16.3%; grade 1: 14.0%, grade 2: 2.3%), decreased appetite (14.0%; all grade 1), and nausea (9.3%; grade 1: 7.0%, grade 2: 2.3%). Diarrhea was infrequent (2.3%; grade 1).

Non-hematological toxicities comprised asthenia/fatigue (18.6%; grade 1: 16.3%, grade 2: 2.3%), palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia syndrome (7.0%; all grade 2), and rash (4.7%; all grade 2). Hepatobiliary disorders featured ALT elevation (9.3%; grade 1: 4.7%, grade 2: 2.3%, grade 3: 2.3%).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This present phase II study is the first to prospectively evaluate the efficacy and safety of a platinum-free triplet regimen (nab-paclitaxel, S-1, and tislelizumab) as first-line therapy in advanced G/GEJ adenocarcinoma. Compared with established platinum-based immunochemotherapy, our regimen demonstrates several critical innovations. First, nab-paclitaxel, a solvent-free formulation, enables higher intratumoral drug delivery and reduced hypersensitivity reactions [22–24]. To balance efficacy with cumulative myelo- and neurotoxicity in a triplet that includes S-1 and an anti-PD-1 antibody, nab-paclitaxel was administered at 100 mg/m² on days 1 and 8 every 21 days. This schedule maintains dose intensity while allowing a 7-day recovery interval, with the aim of preserving immunotherapy adherence in an older, comorbidity-burdened population. The choice was also informed by prior phase II combinations of nab-paclitaxel with fluoropyrimidines in gastrointestinal malignancies that frequently used day 1/8 dosing near 100 mg/m² with acceptable safety and consistent antitumor activity [25–27]. S-1, as an oral fluoropyrimidine, offers both convenience and robust efficacy in East Asian populations, providing a rational non-platinum backbone [28]. Our previous study on the combination therapy of paclitaxel and S-1 in patients with metastatic or locally advanced gastric cancer demonstrated therapeutic activity and acceptable toxicity [29]. Second, the inclusion of tislelizumab, a next-generation PD-1 inhibitor with an optimized Fc domain to minimize FcγR binding, is based on compelling data indicating a lower risk of immune-related adverse events and promising efficacy in gastrointestinal malignancies [30–32]. This mechanism-driven triplet strategy maximizes tumor immunogenicity while minimizing cumulative toxicity, thereby addressing key limitations of platinum-based regimens.

Our study reported an ORR of 81.4% and a median PFS of 8.6 months, which are comparable to ranges reported in recent phase III studies of first-line immunochemotherapy in advanced gastric cancer (ORR: 47.3%-72.6%; PFS: 6.9-10.45 months) [4, 18, 33–40]. In larger randomized studies, including ORIENT-16 and CheckMate 649, the survival benefit associated with PD-1 blockade generally appeared greater in patients with higher PD-L1 expression, particularly those with CPS ≥ 10 [5, 41]. However, this pattern was not reproduced in our cohort. An unexpected was that patients with PD-L1 CPS ≥ 10 did not demonstrate longer PFS or OS than those with PD-L1 CPS < 10 (median PFS 6.7 vs. 14.0 months, P = 0.071). Several factors may account for this discrepancy. First, the sample size was modest, and PD-L1 CPS data were unavailable for a subset of patients, limiting precision and increasing the risk of random variation. Second, conversion surgery was more frequent in some lower-CPS patients, and censoring at the time of surgery in the primary PFS analysis may have influenced subgroup estimates. Third, imbalances in baseline characteristics, including histologic subtype, metastatic burden, and treatment exposure, may have contributed to the observed pattern. Taken together, these considerations suggest that the apparent CPS-related differences in our cohort are likely confounded and should be interpreted cautiously. Rather than indicating a true inverse association, these findings are best regarded as exploratory and hypothesis-generating, and they require confirmation in larger, prospectively stratified studies.

Our cohort also included a substantial proportion of older patients (median age, 63 years; 46.5% aged ≥ 65 years), a population that is often under-represented in randomized studies and may be less tolerant of platinum-based therapy [42–46]. In exploratory subgroup analyses, patients aged ≥ 65 years had longer PFS and OS than those aged < 65 years. Notably, among the long-term survivors with extended follow-up, most were aged ≥ 65 years and several had intestinal-type histology. These findings may reflect a combination of treatment tolerability, selection of fitter older patients within this ECOG 0–1 cohort, and more indolent tumor biology in a subset of older individuals. Accordingly, although patients aged ≥ 65 years had numerically longer PFS and OS in exploratory analyses, this observation should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive given the modest sample size and potential selection bias. Further validation in adequately powered studies will be required to determine whether age identifies a subgroup that may derive particular benefit from this non-platinum regimen.

Clinical data increasingly support the synergistic interaction between taxanes, fluoropyrimidines, and PD-1 blockade [47]. Nab-paclitaxel augments dendritic cell activation and antigen cross-presentation, while S-1 induces immunogenic cell death and upregulates interferon response pathways, thus priming the tumor microenvironment for anti-PD-1 activity [48]. Tislelizumab, with its high specificity for PD-1, further unleashes cytotoxic T-cell function, as evidenced by recent single-arm and randomized studies showing durable responses across GI tumors [49]. Recent reports on chemoimmunotherapy, such as the ATTRACTION-4 and RATIONALE-305 studies, confirm the benefit of PD-1 inhibitors with chemotherapy in Asian patients, yet evidence for regimens that omit platinum remains sparse [4, 18]. Our results address this knowledge gap and support the growing paradigm of tailored, toxicity-sparing, immunogenic chemotherapy.

A particularly noteworthy achievement of this trial is the high conversion surgery rate (18.6%), which not only exceeds most recent chemoimmunotherapy series but also highlights the potential of platinum-sparing strategies to achieve deep tumor regression in metastatic gastric cancer. Historically, conversion surgery has been feasible for only a minority of patients with initially unresectable disease, with rates in recent pivotal studies ranging from 6% to 14% [4, 33]. In our cohort, nearly 1 in 5 patients achieved sufficient downstaging for radical resection, and 2 patients (4.8%) achieved a pathological complete response (pCR), both of whom remained disease-free at last follow-up. Recent large-scale Japanese and Korean studies, such as the CONVO-GC-01 and the KCSG ST19-16, further underscore the importance of conversion surgery for selected metastatic gastric cancer patients, reporting conversion rates around 15%-18%, but with most cases limited to patients with favorable biology or high chemotherapy sensitivity [50, 51]. Our regimen, which produced a conversion rate at the upper end of this spectrum, was notable for including a broad real-world population, including patients with advanced age, retroperitoneal lymph node, and peritoneal metastases.

The prognostic significance of conversion surgery was robustly demonstrated. Patients who underwent surgery experienced a strong trend toward improved overall survival (OS) (median 29.5 months vs. 18.3 months, HR: 0.42, 95% CI: 0.20–0.90, P = 0.050). These findings echo those from retrospective analyses and prospective series demonstrating that surgical resection following effective systemic therapy is associated with improved long-term survival in selected stage IV gastric cancer [52, 53]. Mechanistically, this benefit is thought to derive from the elimination of chemoimmunotherapy-resistant cell clones and restoration of local immune surveillance after macroscopic tumor clearance [54].

Importantly, our results contribute to the evolving paradigm that systemic therapy not only offers palliative benefit but can potentially convert metastatic gastric cancer to a surgically curable state in a meaningful subset of patients. This paradigm shift has profound implications for clinical decision-making and underscores the necessity of multidisciplinary evaluation in the modern management of advanced gastric cancer.

Our findings indicate that a higher baseline neutrophil‑to‑lymphocyte ratio (NLR) (> 3.22) was associated with a trend toward reduced overall survival (16.4 vs. 22.2 months), although this association did not reach statistical significance (Log-Rank P = 0.061). This trend aligns with previous studies that have consistently linked elevated NLR to poorer survival outcomes in various cancers, including gastric adenocarcinoma. The potential prognostic value of NLR may be explained by its reflection of a pro-tumor inflammatory microenvironment, characterized by neutrophil-driven tumor progression and lymphocyte-mediated immunosuppression, facilitating angiogenesis and immune evasion [55, 56]. A recent meta-analysis indicated that an elevated NLR was significantly associated with reduced OS and could serve as a cost-effective prognostic biomarker [57]. Similarly, the association of high NLR with diminished response to immunotherapy has been increasingly recognized, as neutrophil-driven inflammation can restrict T-cell infiltration and function within the tumor microenvironment, thereby limiting the efficacy of checkpoint inhibitors [58, 59]. Although our data did not reveal a statistically significant difference in PFS between the high and low NLR groups, the trend toward shortened PFS observed among patients with elevated NLR aligns well with previous findings and may reflect underlying tumor-immune interactions affecting initial therapeutic responses [57]. Given these cumulative insights, baseline NLR emerges as a promising stratification tool to optimize therapeutic decision-making, allowing clinicians to identify patients at higher risk for poorer outcomes who may benefit from intensified surveillance or adjunctive therapeutic approaches.

Our regimen displayed an acceptable and manageable safety profile. Hematological toxicities were most frequent, in line with expectations for taxane- and fluoropyrimidine-based therapies. However, severe non-hematological toxicities were rare, and treatment discontinuation for toxicity was infrequent. Grade ≥ 3 haematologic AEs were infrequent with nab-paclitaxel/S-1/tislelizumab (neutropenia 9.3%; leukopenia 7.0%; anaemia 2.3%; thrombocytopenia 2.3%). Contemporary PD-1 + platinum doublets report grade 3–4 neutropenia around 12–15% [5], whereas cisplatin‑based combinations historically report higher rates, often 20–40% depending on backbone [60]. These data suggest that a nab‑paclitaxel/S‑1 backbone may offer a more tolerable alternative for patients who are older or have comorbidities that limit cisplatin use. These results are consistent with the improved safety profile of taxane-based chemoimmunotherapy without platinum recently reported in both clinical trials and real-world settings [61].

This single-arm, single-centre study enrolled a modest sample; consequently, any subgroup comparisons are underpowered and should be regarded as exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Estimates are imprecise and may be influenced by random variation and multiple testing. While our findings are encouraging and suggest a paradigm shift toward more individualized, toxicity-conscious front-line strategies, further randomized trials are necessary to establish superiority or non-inferiority versus platinum-based regimens. Exploration of predictive biomarkers (including PD-L1 expression and molecular subtypes) will be crucial to optimize patient selection and maximize benefit [62].

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our study demonstrates that the combination of nab-paclitaxel, S-1, and tislelizumab provides a highly active, well-tolerated, and innovative first-line regimen for advanced gastric or G/GEJ adenocarcinoma. It is characterized by a high response rate, exceptional conversion surgery feasibility, and favorable long-term survival. Our study sets the stage for further investigation of platinum-sparing immunochemotherapy. This approach deserves consideration in future clinical paradigms, especially for older patients who may be vulnerable to platinum-associated toxicities.
